title: A forest can grow more than food.
imageAlt: A flourishing mixed agroforestry landscape in Guatemala
summary: What ARC’s community-based approach tells us about growing resilience from the ground up.
paragraphs: A food forest brings trees, crops, soil, and people into a living relationship. It offers a different way to think about a farm: as a diverse ecosystem that can nourish a community while caring for the land.

Agroforestry Regeneration Communities began in April 2021. Its documented approach connects smallholder farmers with experienced teachers, taking learning into the communities where it will be used. Local access matters: people should not have to travel far or pay large course fees to learn practical skills.

AEF’s archived project page describes work in Malawi, Guatemala, Uganda, and the Caribbean Islands. The results it reports belong to this wider partner network. Clear attribution helps us appreciate both the people doing the work and the support that makes learning possible.
The lasting story is about capacity: people building knowledge, relationships, and confidence that can continue to grow beyond an individual grant.

title: The next generation is already growing change.
imageAlt: Youth in Permaculture Prize recipient Brenda Nakafeero
summary: A look back at youth-led kitchen gardens, learning spaces, and the power of practical support.
paragraphs: Young people are already creating practical responses to the challenges around them. AEF’s Youth in Permaculture Prize archive brings together stories of school gardens, native-forest planting, local food systems, and community learning.

One of those young leaders is Brenda Nakafeero, a 2022 recipient in northern Uganda. The archived profile describes her work teaching permaculture to young women and single mothers, and helping establish kitchen gardens at home.

Her award was intended to support a learning center, a tool library, a local seed-exchange network, and water security for food projects. These were the plans recorded at the time of the award; they should not be read as a current completion report.
Such stories show why accessible funding and mentorship matter. An investment in one local leader can create new opportunities for other people to learn and participate.

title: From climate concern to creative confidence.
imageAlt: Students observing plants in an educational program shared by Eco-Designers
summary: How practical environmental education gives young people a way to take part.
paragraphs: Environmental education becomes more powerful when learners can do something with it. Beyond Organic Design connects permaculture design with hands-on experiences, helping young people see their own ability to shape their surroundings.

AEF’s 2025 homepage describes BOD’s Eco-Designers program: a customizable curriculum accompanied by professional development for educators. The idea is to help schools adapt the learning to their own students and places.

The archived page reports that more than 6,165 young people had participated in BOD’s courses. That is the organization’s cumulative reported reach, rather than a claim that all of those places were funded by AEF.
The opportunity is larger than any single lesson. Learning to observe, collaborate, and design with nature can give young people constructive ways to respond to an uncertain future.
